claims.text: The baseline alloy is compositionally similar to HfMoTaTiZr.
As-built additively manufactured HfMoTaTiZr-like components exhibit dimensional distortion and mechanical weaknesses.
Rapid solidification and inherent processing defects cause the baseline components' dimensional and mechanical problems.
The intervention is addition of approximately 4–5 at% Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr-like feedstock.
Approximately 4.2 at% Cr causes a Laves phase to form in addition to the BCC phase.
The Cr-induced Laves phase is fine and reticulated at grain boundaries.
Cr addition reduces the BCC lattice parameters.
Cr dissolves in the BCC phase, produces lattice distortion, and thereby causes solid-solution hardening.
Cr promotes controlled nucleation of a fine Laves phase.
The combination of solid-solution hardening and Laves-phase formation offsets rapid thermal gradients and residual stresses during additive manufacturing.
The proposed mechanism reduces fabrication-induced defects and increases resistance to crack propagation.
Cr-modified additively manufactured components will have lower dimensional deviation and residual stress than unmodified components.
Cr-modified components will have greater hardness and yield strength than unmodified components.
Cr-modified components will have greater fracture toughness than unmodified components.
The hardness improvement under additive manufacturing may be of the same approximate order as the reported 50–60% enhancement in vacuum-arc-melted material.
Vacuum-arc-melted HfMoTaTiZr containing 4.2 at% Cr reached a reported hardness of 535.8 HV0.3 and a reported yield strength of 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa.
The intervention should work only when additive-manufacturing cooling rates and thermal gradients permit controlled secondary-phase formation.
Extreme additive-manufacturing conditions that generate substantially different microstructures may eliminate the proposed benefits.
The cited evidence was obtained by vacuum arc melting under inert gas rather than by additive manufacturing.
Different thermal histories and phase evolution make transfer of the vacuum-arc-melting results to additive manufacturing uncertain.
